interview.a: There are 32−26 = 6 host bits, so 2^6 = 64 total addresses; a conventional subnet generally has 62 usable host addresses.

interview.q: What is longest-prefix match?
interview.a: A router chooses the most specific matching route, meaning the route with the greatest prefix length.

title: HTTPS
summary: HTTP over TLS. Confidentiality, integrity, and (usually) server authentication.
what: HTTPS carries HTTP messages over a TLS-protected connection, commonly using TCP and TLS 1.3 or 1.2, or QUIC/TLS for HTTP/3. TLS authenticates the server using certificates and protects application data against network observation and modification when configured correctly.
why: HTTPS protects credentials, session cookies, API requests, and page content over untrusted networks. It does not guarantee that a website is honest, that the browser is malware-free, or that a compromised server keeps its own data safe.
mental: TLS establishes cryptographic keys and verifies the server's identity against a certificate and requested hostname. HTTP then travels inside the protected channel, rather than as readable application bytes on the network.
points: A certificate chain links the server certificate to a trust anchor in the client trust store.
Hostname validation and certificate validity dates matter; encryption without correct identity checks can protect a connection to the wrong party.
TLS provides confidentiality and integrity for data in transit and authenticates the server in ordinary web usage.
HTTP status codes and API semantics remain application-layer concerns; TLS does not make a broken API correct.
Secure cookie flags, HSTS, authorization, and input validation solve different problems and complement HTTPS.
steps: The browser resolves the hostname and connects to the server.
The client and server negotiate TLS parameters and validate certificates.
They establish traffic keys and protect subsequent records.
The browser sends the HTTP request inside the protected channel and checks the response.
usage: Protecting logins, cookies, and API traffic.
Explaining certificates, trust chains, and browser security warnings.
Distinguishing transport security from application authorization.
mistakes: Assuming the padlock proves a business is legitimate.
Ignoring certificate hostname errors or telling users to bypass them.
Treating HTTPS as a replacement for access control or secure application code.

interview.q: What security properties does HTTPS provide?
interview.a: TLS can provide confidentiality and integrity in transit and normally authenticates the server name through certificate validation.

interview.q: Does HTTPS prevent SQL injection?
interview.a: No. It protects data in transit; SQL injection must be prevented by safe query construction, typically parameterized queries, and appropriate database permissions.

title: Ethernet
summary: The LAN technology: CSMA/CD history, switching present, 802.3 framing.
what: Ethernet is a family of wired local-network technologies standardized mainly under IEEE 802.3. Modern switched full-duplex Ethernet links use frames and MAC addressing, while collision detection belongs primarily to the historical shared-medium/half-duplex model.
why: Ethernet provides a common link-layer framing and delivery technology for local networks. Understanding frame boundaries, MAC addresses, VLAN tagging, and switches helps diagnose local connectivity independently of IP routing.
mental: An Ethernet frame is the envelope used for one local-link hop. A switch learns which MAC addresses are reachable through its ports and forwards known unicast frames toward the appropriate port.
points: A frame contains destination and source MAC addresses, a type/length field, payload, and frame-check sequence.
Switches learn source MAC addresses and associate them with ingress ports in a forwarding database.
Unknown unicast and broadcast frames may be flooded within a VLAN, subject to switch behavior and policy.
VLANs divide a physical switching fabric into logically separate layer-2 broadcast domains.
Full-duplex switched Ethernet avoids the collisions described by classic CSMA/CD shared-medium Ethernet.
steps: Host A sends a frame addressed to Host B's MAC address.
The switch records A's source MAC on the incoming port.
If B's MAC is known in the same VLAN, the switch forwards only to B's port.
If unknown, the switch may flood the frame within the VLAN and learn B when it replies.
usage: Troubleshooting link state, VLAN membership, and unexpected broadcasts.
Reading packet captures and switch forwarding tables.
Distinguishing local Ethernet forwarding from IP routing.
mistakes: Saying modern switched full-duplex Ethernet still relies on collision detection in the same way as shared coaxial Ethernet.
Assuming a switch routes traffic between IP subnets without a layer-3 function.
Confusing MAC addresses with IP addresses or port numbers.

interview.q: What information does a basic Ethernet switch use to forward frames?
interview.a: It primarily uses the destination MAC address and its learned forwarding database within the relevant VLAN.

interview.q: When does an Ethernet switch flood a frame?
interview.a: For broadcast traffic and often for unknown unicast or multicast according to its configuration and protocol behavior, within the relevant VLAN.

title: ARP
summary: Resolve IPv4 to MAC on a LAN. The cache, the timeout, and the spoof.
what: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) discovers the layer-2 MAC address associated with an IPv4 address on the local link. A host broadcasts a request asking which device owns an IP address; the owner typically replies with its MAC address.
why: IP routing needs a frame for the next local hop. When the destination is off-subnet, ARP resolves the gateway's MAC address rather than resolving the remote server's MAC directly.
mental: IP chooses where a packet should go at the network layer; ARP finds the local Ethernet envelope recipient for the next hop. The answer is normally cached briefly to avoid broadcasting for every packet.
points: ARP is for IPv4 on a local broadcast domain; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery.
An ARP request is normally broadcast, while the response is usually unicast to the requester.
ARP cache entries can be stale and refreshed; static and dynamic entries have different management properties.
ARP is not authenticated by default, which enables spoofing on a local network without additional protections.
ARP does not cross routers as a normal broadcast; each routed hop resolves its own next-hop address.
steps: A host wants to send to a remote IPv4 destination.
It checks the routing table and chooses the default gateway as next hop.
If the gateway MAC is not in the ARP cache, the host broadcasts an ARP request for the gateway's IP.
The gateway replies with its MAC; the host sends an Ethernet frame to that MAC with the remote IP packet as payload.
usage: Debugging a same-subnet host that cannot be reached.
Understanding gateway MAC resolution and ARP caches.
Assessing local-network spoofing risks and mitigations.
mistakes: Trying to ARP for a remote internet server instead of the local gateway.
Assuming an ARP reply is cryptographically authenticated.
Confusing ARP cache problems with DNS resolution failures.

interview.q: If a server is on another subnet, whose MAC does the host resolve?
interview.a: The host normally resolves the next-hop router/default gateway's MAC, while the IP destination remains the remote server.

interview.q: Why is ARP spoofing possible?
interview.a: Basic ARP replies are not authenticated cryptographically, so a local attacker may send false IP-to-MAC mappings unless protections detect or prevent it.

title: DHCP
summary: Automatic host configuration: address, mask, gateway, DNS, lease.
what: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) automatically supplies network configuration such as an IP address, subnet mask/prefix, default gateway, DNS resolvers, and lease timing. DHCPv4 commonly uses UDP ports 67 and 68 and the discover-offer-request-acknowledge exchange.
why: Manual addressing does not scale well and creates conflicting configurations. DHCP centralizes allocation and reduces mistakes, while leases allow addresses to be reused when clients leave.
mental: Think of DHCP as a time-limited address lease from a network administrator. A client requests configuration, a server offers a lease, the client requests it, and the server confirms the parameters.
points: The familiar DHCPv4 DORA sequence is Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.
A lease has a duration; clients renew before expiry under the protocol's timing rules.
DHCP options convey more than the address itself, including gateway and DNS configuration.
A rogue or compromised DHCP server can give malicious gateway or resolver settings.
DHCP broadcasts stay within their local broadcast domain unless a relay forwards requests to a server elsewhere.
steps: A new client joins a LAN without a usable IPv4 configuration.
It broadcasts DHCP Discover; one or more servers may send Offers.
The client requests one offered configuration and the chosen server sends an Acknowledgement.
The client configures its interface and later renews the lease as needed.
usage: Investigating a host with no address, wrong gateway, or wrong DNS server.
Understanding DHCP relay in multi-subnet networks.
Planning address pools, reservations, lease periods, and conflict handling.
mistakes: Assuming DHCP itself resolves human-readable hostnames; DNS does that.
Assuming a DHCP offer proves the server is trusted.
Checking only the assigned IP and ignoring the mask, gateway, DNS, lease, and duplicate-address state.

interview.q: What does DORA stand for in DHCPv4?
interview.a: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

interview.q: Why use a DHCP relay?
interview.a: It forwards client DHCP messages across a routed boundary to a server, because local broadcasts do not normally cross routers.

title: Congestion Control
summary: Protecting the network from collapse: slow start, AIMD, ECN, and BBR.
what: Congestion control adapts a sender's transmission rate to estimated network capacity and congestion. TCP algorithms infer congestion from signals such as loss, delay, or explicit congestion notification; designs differ in how they probe capacity and reduce sending rate.
why: Without congestion control, senders can inject more traffic than links and routers can handle, increasing queues, delay, retransmissions, and loss for many flows. Congestion control balances throughput with stability and sharing.
mental: Flow control protects the receiver from being overwhelmed; congestion control protects the path. A sender must respect both the receiver's advertised window and its congestion window.
points: TCP's congestion window limits outstanding data in flight; the receiver window expresses receiver-side capacity.
Slow start probes available capacity rapidly from a small initial window, within the algorithm's current behavior.
AIMD-style algorithms increase cautiously and reduce on congestion signals, while modern algorithms may use different models.
Packet loss can indicate congestion but can also have other causes; algorithms use timing and protocol-specific signals.
Fairness is a property of competing flows and paths, not a guarantee that every connection receives identical throughput.
steps: A sender starts with a conservative congestion window.
Successful acknowledgements permit the window to grow according to the algorithm.
A congestion signal such as loss or ECN causes a reduction or a model update.
The sender probes again while staying within the receiver's advertised window.
usage: Explaining throughput collapse, queueing delay, and TCP behavior.
Distinguishing congestion control from receiver flow control.
Comparing different TCP congestion-control algorithms using measured workload results.
mistakes: Treating the receiver window and congestion window as the same control.
Assuming every dropped packet proves congestion.
Comparing algorithms without accounting for RTT, bottlenecks, competing flows, and test conditions.

interview.q: How does flow control differ from congestion control?
interview.a: Flow control protects the receiver from excessive in-flight data; congestion control adapts sending to the network path's capacity.

interview.q: What role does ECN play?
interview.a: Where supported and negotiated, Explicit Congestion Notification lets network devices mark packets to signal congestion without relying solely on packet drops.
